ocar.opportunity: Hue is a derived color percept, not a photoreceptor channel. Finding hue-selective cells in a genetically and connectomically tractable optic lobe would let circuit mechanisms of narrow color tuning be tested rather than inferred from primate cortex alone.
ocar.challenge: Flies have four spectral photoreceptor channels and known color-opponent signals at R7/R8 terminals, but chromatic responses of downstream neurons had not been described, so it was unclear how opponent signals become hue-like.
ocar.action: Christenson, Sanz Diez, Heath, Saavedra-Weisenhaus, Adachi, Nern, Abbott, and Behnia, in Nature Neuroscience (2024), measure candidate optic-lobe neurons across fly color space, build a connectomics-constrained circuit model from a whole-brain EM volume, and genetically perturb recurrence in adults.
ocar.resolution: They report hue-selective neurons in the Drosophila optic lobe. The model accounts for that selectivity only when recurrent connections are included, and adult genetic manipulations that perturb recurrence confirm the prediction. The authors present this as a circuit basis for hue selectivity in color vision.
ocar.future_work: The discussion hypothesizes that the same recurrent motif may be a foundation for hue selectivity in other brains, including primates; that comparative claim is not tested here.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies have cells in their visual system that care about hue, not just raw wavelength. A wiring-based model plus genetic tests says the key is looping connections, not a one-way chain from the eye.
summaries.intermediate: Christenson and colleagues (Nature Neuroscience, 2024) identify hue-selective neurons in the Drosophila optic lobe. Color vision starts in pale and yellow R7/R8 photoreceptors (opsins Rh3–Rh6) whose terminals already carry color-opponent signals. Using a whole-brain EM volume, they build a connectomics-constrained model of downstream circuitry and find that recurrence is required for narrow hue tuning; genetic perturbation of recurrence in adult flies supports that prediction. Flies are treated as a circuit-level model of the physical-to-perceptual color transform (hue, saturation, brightness).
summaries.advanced: Hue-selective cell-type names and quantitative tuning widths are not in the selected extract (the introduction cuts off at ‘responses of three’). Recurrence is a model prediction confirmed by adult genetic perturbation, not a claim that feedforward circuitry is absent. Cross-species ‘foundational basis’ language in the discussion is a hypothesis. The extract is the published Nature Neuroscience article.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies have cells in their visual system that care about hue, not just raw wavelength. A wiring-based model plus genetic tests says the key is looping connections, not a one-way chain from the eye.

ocar.opportunity: Hemisphere- or whole-brain axon tracing at cellular resolution cannot wait on dense expert labels, yet topology of the traces is what connectivity analysis needs.
ocar.challenge: Supervised 3D U-Nets for axon segmentation still depend on labor-intensive labels, and generic self-supervised puzzles may not preserve centerlines.
ocar.action: Xu, Shamsi, Gjesteby, and Brattain, at IEEE/CVF WACV (2024), pretrain 3D U-Nets on mouse-brain volumes with a self-supervised edge-detector reconstruction task, then fine-tune for axon segmentation and centerline detection on a different mouse dataset, comparing against slice-permutation and Rubik’s-cube pretraining.
ocar.resolution: Edge-detection pretraining improved the baseline’s segmentation, topology preservation, and centerline detection by up to 5.03%, 4.65%, and 5.41%, respectively. Slice-permutation and Rubik’s-cube pretraining did not consistently beat the baseline. The edge task was also less sensitive to the SSL hyperparameter k than slice permutation.
ocar.future_work: The authors flag Canny-parameter choice as an unsolved SSL design issue and suggest reconstructing a parameter-free edge or skeleton map. They hypothesize that noise in Dataset 1 hurt the puzzle tasks on Dataset 2.

summaries.beginner: Tracing axons through huge 3D brain images usually needs experts to paint labels. Teaching the network first to redraw edges, without those labels, made axon maps and centerlines more accurate and better connected.
summaries.intermediate: Xu, Shamsi, Gjesteby, and Brattain (WACV, 2024) propose self-supervised reconstruction of an edge detector as pretraining for topology-oriented 3D axon segmentation and centerline detection. 3D U-Nets were pretrained on one mouse-brain dataset (edge, slice-order, or Rubik’s cube) and evaluated on another. Relative to a non-pretrained baseline, the edge task improved segmentation, topology preservation, and centerline detection by up to 5.03%, 4.65%, and 5.41%. Puzzle-style SSL did not consistently help. Mouse volumes came from Kwanghun Chung’s laboratory.
summaries.advanced: Percentage gains are the authors’ stated maxima, not a single held-out leaderboard. SSL input sizes tested include 128×128×32 and 192×192×48. Downstream performance may depend on Canny parameters. Dataset-1 artifacts are offered as a reason puzzle methods underperformed. IEEE Xplore copy.

plain_language_summary: Tracing axons through huge 3D brain images usually needs experts to paint labels. Teaching the network first to redraw edges, without those labels, made axon maps and centerlines more accurate and better connected.

ocar.opportunity: The hippocampal mossy-fiber bouton is large enough for direct presynaptic recording, so biophysics of transmission and plasticity can be tied to a synapse sitting at the center of the trisynaptic memory circuit.
ocar.challenge: The detonator or teacher-synapse picture of mossy fibers has been hard to test, and how vesicle-pool organization and calcium-channel coupling shape network computations such as pattern separation and completion remains unsettled.
ocar.action: Vandael and Jonas, in Science (2024), as described in the catalog abstract, review nanoanatomy and nanophysiology of the hippocampal mossy-fiber synapse, including presynaptic patch clamp, paired recording, super-resolution light microscopy, and freeze-fracture and flash-and-freeze EM.
ocar.resolution: The abstract links facilitation to coupling between Ca2+ channels and release sensors, and potentiation to vesicle-pool size and organization. At the network level the synapse is argued to contribute not only to storage but also to recall, pattern separation, and pattern completion, with structural plasticity as a candidate synaptic engram. Disease sections flag mossy-fiber sprouting in epilepsy, synaptopathy in genetic psychiatric models, and early involvement in neurodegenerative memory loss.
ocar.future_work: The outlook treats complete biophysical, network, and disease understanding of this synapse, and selective therapy, as an agenda rather than a finished result.

summaries.beginner: A giant synapse in the hippocampus is famous as a possible detonator for memory circuits. This review gathers new nanoscale anatomy and physiology of that connection and asks how its physics shapes learning and disease.
summaries.intermediate: Vandael and Jonas (Science, 2024) review the dentate-gyrus-to-CA3 mossy-fiber synapse. Per the catalog abstract, its size enables presynaptic recording comparable to the squid giant synapse or the calyx of Held. Facilitation is tied to Ca2+-channel–sensor coupling and potentiation to vesicle pools; network roles include storage, recall, pattern separation, and completion. Disease discussion covers epilepsy-related sprouting, psychiatric synaptopathy, and early neurodegenerative impairment. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Hayashi, Ohno, Molnár, and Toida, iScience (2026), on presynaptic SNAP25 in mossy-fiber–CA3 maturation, not the Vandael and Jonas Science review. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Science paper is required for figures and primary citations.

plain_language_summary: A giant synapse in the hippocampus is famous as a possible detonator for memory circuits. This review gathers new nanoscale anatomy and physiology of that connection and asks how its physics shapes learning and disease.

ocar.opportunity: Strong-gradient human MRI (Connectome 2.0 class, ≲500 mT/m) makes axonal-diameter mapping tempting, if the finite transverse diffusivity at high b can be read as a caliber.
ocar.challenge: Real axons are not straight impermeable cylinders: microscopy shows beading (caliber variation) and undulation, both known to bias diameter estimates, including in pathology.
ocar.action: Lee, Tian, Sheft, Coronado-Leija, Ramos-Llordén, Abdollahzadeh, Fieremans, Novikov, and Huang, in NMR in Biomedicine (2024), run Monte Carlo diffusion simulations in axons reconstructed from 3D EM of a human temporal-lobe specimen, using sequence parameters matched to Connectome 2.0.
ocar.resolution: Diameter recovery is accurate for nonbeaded, nonundulating fibers. With realistic caliber variation and undulation, diameter is heavily underestimated because of beading, and that underestimation overshadows the known overestimation from undulation. The authors attribute the underestimation to variations in coarse-grained axial diffusivity. Pathological beading and undulation (e.g. TBI, ischemia) would therefore confound interpretation of apparent diameter change.
ocar.future_work: Relevance to in vivo mapping needs multimodality validation. Alternative encodings, multiple diffusion times, higher-order harmonics, or extra MRI contrasts are suggested as ways to disentangle the biases.

summaries.beginner: MRI can try to guess axon thickness from how water wiggles. Simulations in real human axons from electron microscopy show that bumps and wiggles in the axon itself can make those guesses too small, which matters when reading disease scans.
summaries.intermediate: Lee and colleagues (NMR in Biomedicine, 2024) simulate diffusion MRI in 3D-EM-segmented human temporal-lobe axons with Connectome 2.0–class gradients (≲500 mT/m). Straight cylinders recover diameter; realistic beading underestimates it enough to dominate the overestimation caused by undulation. The spherical-mean signal is the mapping readout. Pathological white-matter studies that interpret diameter change should treat caliber variation and undulation as confounders. The PDF is a PMC author manuscript.
summaries.advanced: Simulations are in fixed human tissue geometries, not live brains—the conclusions say in vivo relevance is unproven. The ≲500 mT/m figure is the scanner’s stated max gradient, not a measured in vivo protocol. Figure 1a is adapted from Shapson-Coe et al. Diameter ‘heavily underestimated’ is qualitative in the extract; per-fiber millimetre values live in figures not captured here.

plain_language_summary: MRI can try to guess axon thickness from how water wiggles. Simulations in real human axons from electron microscopy show that bumps and wiggles in the axon itself can make those guesses too small, which matters when reading disease scans.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes of identified neurons can show whether experience rewires a circuit, not only whether activity weights change, if the same synapses can be scored across animals and conditions.
ocar.challenge: Sample sizes of EM connectomes have limited population analyses of wiring variation, and how associative learning anatomically restructures adult circuits is poorly known.
ocar.action: Tang, Lee, Cook, Ho, Potter, and Bülow, in Current Biology (2023), map the lateralized C. elegans salt circuit (ASE–AWC) with synaptic reporters, behavior, and genetics, including an ASE>AWC iBLINC reporter and insulin-pathway manipulations.
ocar.resolution: Naive animals prefer the salt concentration experienced with food via a left-biased network (ASEL>AWC stronger than ASER>AWC). Conditioning at elevated salt adds synapses that flip the bias to ASER>AWC, driven by asymmetric paracrine insulin signaling. The authors argue this anatomical flip, with known ASE/AWC polarity onto AIA/AIB/AIY, can reverse chemotactic preference. They note glutamatergic ASER–AIB modulation as a parallel, non-exclusive mechanism.
ocar.future_work: Whether rewiring of asymmetric circuits is a conserved learning motif (they mention bird song and Drosophila asymmetric structures) is speculation. Connectome variability more generally may be experience-driven; that claim is opened, not fully quantified, in the extract.

summaries.beginner: Worms remember the salt level they ate at by physically adding synapses and flipping which side of a paired circuit talks louder. Insulin signals from one cell to another drive that rewiring.
summaries.intermediate: Tang, Lee, Cook, Ho, Potter, and Bülow (Current Biology, 2023) show that the C. elegans ASE–AWC salt circuit is anatomically plastic. Naive left-biased ASEL→AWC connectivity becomes right-biased ASER→AWC after high-salt-with-food conditioning, via new synapses and asymmetric paracrine insulin. Behavior is interpreted through known excitatory/inhibitory projections onto AIA, AIB, and AIY. The paper treats experience-dependent connectome change as fundamental to this associative learning. PMC author manuscript.
summaries.advanced: This is light-microscopic synaptic labeling and genetics, not a new whole-animal EM connectome. Insulin is identified as necessary for the anatomical flip; other salt-learning mechanisms (e.g. ASER–AIB glutamate) are explicitly not excluded. ‘Conserved mechanism’ for lateralized learning is a discussion speculation. Catalog dataset tag is White+ C. elegans; this work is live imaging of a defined synapse class.

plain_language_summary: Worms remember the salt level they ate at by physically adding synapses and flipping which side of a paired circuit talks louder. Insulin signals from one cell to another drive that rewiring.

ocar.opportunity: If the mammalian primary rod pathway existed before mammals, its cell types and wiring should be recoverable in a distant vertebrate such as zebrafish.
ocar.challenge: The rod bipolar cell (RBC) pathway—rods onto dedicated BCs, then onto a stereotyped amacrine network—has been treated as a mammalian invention.
ocar.action: Hellevik, Mardoum, Hahn, and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2023), combine zebrafish single-cell RNA-seq, electrophysiology, histology, and ultrastructural reconstruction of rod bipolar cells, comparing them to mammalian RBCs.
ocar.resolution: Two zebrafish BC types (RBC1/2) are related to mammalian RBCs. Both contact all rods and red cones in their dendritic territory and output largely onto amacrine cells. Amacrine wiring postsynaptic to RBC1 is strikingly like the mammalian primary rod pathway, implying that pathway originated more than ~400 million years ago, before teleost–amniote divergence. RBC2 forms a separate pathway, either lost in mammals or a fish addition.
ocar.future_work: Functional roles unique to RBC2 remain unknown. The extract’s later pages are methods/references, so species-by-species molecular homologies should be checked in the figures and supplements.

summaries.beginner: Night vision in mammals was thought to use a special retinal circuit invented in our lineage. A zebrafish study finds two rod bipolar cell types, one wired much like the mammalian night pathway, so that design is probably ancient.
summaries.intermediate: Hellevik et al. (bioRxiv, 4 October 2023 version) argue that the primary rod pathway predates mammals. scRNA-seq identifies two zebrafish bipolar types related to mammalian rod BCs. EM, histology, and physiology show both types contact all rods and red cones in their dendritic fields and synapse mainly onto amacrines; RBC1’s amacrine partners resemble the mammalian AII-centered pathway, whereas RBC2 is a separate stream. Divergence from extant mammals is given as ~400 million years. This is a preprint.
summaries.advanced: ‘Conserved in zebrafish’ is a homology-plus-wiring argument, not a claim of identical night-vision behavior. ‘All rods and red-cones in their dendritic territory’ is the authors’ completeness statement for reconstructed cells. The selected extract does not include a synapse census table. Catalog datasets include mouse retina and zebrafish; mouse enters as the mammalian comparison, not as a new mouse volume here.

plain_language_summary: Night vision in mammals was thought to use a special retinal circuit invented in our lineage. A zebrafish study finds two rod bipolar cell types, one wired much like the mammalian night pathway, so that design is probably ancient.

ocar.opportunity: Context-dependent action sequences might use one motor pathway in two dynamical regimes rather than duplicated, context-specific circuits.
ocar.challenge: How recent sensory history switches song patterning—simple one-mode trains far from a female versus complex pulse–sine alternation nearby—was not mapped from brain to ventral nerve cord in Drosophila.
ocar.action: Roemschied, Pacheco, Aragon, Ireland, Li, Thieringer, Pang, and Murthy, in Nature (2023), combine physiology, genetics, and a compact circuit model of the male song pathway, including pC2, descending pIP10, P1a, and VNC premotor nodes.
ocar.resolution: VNC song circuitry implements mutual inhibition and rebound excitability between pulse- and sine-driving nodes. Brief or weak pC2→pIP10 drive yields simple (mostly pulse) song when far; stronger, longer drive also recruits P1a-mediated disinhibition of the VNC core, unlocking complex pulse–sine bouts when near. Female proximity thus selects which repertoire descending commands can access. A reduced model reproduces natural context-dependent dynamics.
ocar.future_work: The authors offer the motif as a template for context-dependent vocalization in songbirds and primates. Acute (milliseconds–seconds) P1a gating is distinguished from P1a’s minutes-long arousal role; how those timescales interact is not fully dissected in the extract.

summaries.beginner: A male fruit fly sings simple notes from far away and mixed songs up close. The same descending pathway does both: extra brain cells unlock a more flexible spinal-like circuit only when the female is near.
summaries.intermediate: Roemschied et al. (Nature, 2023) show that Drosophila courtship song uses one brain-to-VNC pathway in two regimes. Mutual inhibition plus rebound excitability in VNC pulse and sine nodes generate alternation. Weak/brief pC2 and pIP10 activity drives simple song; prolonged input recruits P1a disinhibition so the same descending command produces complex bouts. Catalog tags include the FANC/MANC VNC datasets as the anatomical setting. Open-access Nature article.
summaries.advanced: ‘Simple’ versus ‘complex’ are behavioral categories (one mode versus pulse–sine alternation), not EM completeness claims. The reduced model is sufficient for reported song statistics, not a whole-VNC connectome simulation. P1a has both acute gating and persistent arousal roles; do not collapse them. Dataset DS07 is a catalog tag; this paper is functional circuit analysis.

plain_language_summary: A male fruit fly sings simple notes from far away and mixed songs up close. The same descending pathway does both: extra brain cells unlock a more flexible spinal-like circuit only when the female is near.

ocar.opportunity: Self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled EM volumes could supply the local structure cues that instance segmentation needs when annotations are sparse.
ocar.challenge: Many EM pretraining recipes emphasize high-level semantics or simple reconstruction and miss multiscale, voxel-level consistency of membranes and organelles.
ocar.action: Chen, Huang, Liu, Deng, Chen, and Xiong (arXiv 2308.09917; ICASSP 2024 catalog DOI) pretrain a Siamese network with strong/weak augmentations, voxel reconstruction, cross-attention feature matching, and feature-pyramid contrast, on four large-scale EM datasets, then fine-tune for neuron and mitochondria instance segmentation.
ocar.resolution: The authors report significant gains on those downstream tasks, especially with limited fine-tuning data, attributing them to joint voxel- and feature-level consistency. Code is released (MS-Con-EM-Seg).
ocar.future_work: Numeric margins versus named baselines live in tables not captured in the selected extract; those should be read before treating the method as SOTA.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope pictures of neurons are hard to outline because labels are scarce and the shapes are fiddly. This method first teaches a network to agree with itself at many zoom levels on unlabeled volumes, then uses that skill to segment cells and mitochondria.
summaries.intermediate: Chen et al. (arXiv v3, 5 Sep 2023; catalog venue ICASSP 2024) introduce multiscale-consistency pretraining for EM instance segmentation. A Siamese CNN or Transformer backbone sees strong and weak augmentations; losses include voxel reconstruction, cross-attention matching, and pyramid contrast. After pretraining on four large EM datasets, they report improved neuron and mitochondria segmentation with limited labels. Code: https://github.com/ydchen0806/MS-Con-EM-Seg.
summaries.advanced: The extract is an arXiv CS.CV preprint; page-level ICASSP pagination is not shown. ‘Significant gains’ is the authors’ claim; no percentage is stated in the selected text—do not invent one. Dataset names and split sizes are in omitted tables. Catalog DOI is IEEE ICASSP 2024.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope pictures of neurons are hard to outline because labels are scarce and the shapes are fiddly. This method first teaches a network to agree with itself at many zoom levels on unlabeled volumes, then uses that skill to segment cells and mitochondria.

ocar.opportunity: Behavior is neuromechanical: circuit maps alone cannot explain motion unless muscle mechanics and body physics are in the same account.
ocar.challenge: Integrating connectomics, kinematics, and physical models in a freely behaving animal is rare; larval crawling is offered as a tractable case.
ocar.action: Kohsaka, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2023), reviews Drosophila larval locomotion: interneurons that coordinate intra- and inter-segment muscle activity, exploratory circuits, interspecific diversity, and soft-robot copies of crawling.
ocar.resolution: The review concludes that larval crawling kinematics can be parameterized and that forces, elasticity, and viscosity have been measured well enough to build quantitative neuromechanical models. Connectomics and imaging of population activity inform how locomotion is regulated during exploration. Soft robots are presented as a synthetic test of the same mechanics.
ocar.future_work: Despite identified key interneurons, circuit knowledge is still incomplete. The piece is a framework for other species, not a new reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: A crawling maggot is both a wiring diagram and a soft machine. This review says you need the nerves and the physics of the body together if you want to explain how the animal actually moves.
summaries.intermediate: Kohsaka (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2023) reviews neuromechanics of Drosophila larval locomotion. Topics include central-pattern-generator-like interneuron coordination within and between segments, exploratory circuit control, measured kinematics and material properties, interspecific diversity, and bio-inspired soft robots. The catalog tags the larval Drosophila connectome as the circuit backdrop. The article is a review, not a new EM volume.
summaries.advanced: No new synapse counts are claimed. ‘Ideal model’ is a framing judgment. Soft-robot results are cited as complementary synthesis, not as biological proof. Single-author review.

plain_language_summary: A crawling maggot is both a wiring diagram and a soft machine. This review says you need the nerves and the physics of the body together if you want to explain how the animal actually moves.

ocar.opportunity: Primary cilia are signaling antennae; mapping what they touch in a complete cortical EM volume would show how non-synaptic and synaptic environments reach each cell type.
ocar.challenge: Ciliopathies implicate cilia in circuit disorders, but human cortical cilia had not been placed in a layer-resolved contactome or connectome.
ocar.action: Wu, Cho, Descant, and colleagues, in Neuron (2024 issue of a 2023 paper), reconstruct neuronal and astrocytic primary cilia across all layers of a 1 mm³ serial-section EM volume of human temporal cortex (Lichtman/Shapson-Coe collaboration).
ocar.resolution: Cilia show layer- and cell-type-specific size, shape, axoneme structure, and contact patterns. Neuronal cilium length correlates positively with contact number. A subset of neuronal cilia sit at synaptic clefts, which the authors call a tetrapartite synapse (pre, post, astrocyte, cilium), with more synaptic associations than length-matched axonal controls. Each cell is argued to have a unique ciliary barcode of access to surrounding circuitry.
ocar.future_work: How ciliary receptors transduce those contacts into circuit-level function, and how this organization fails in schizophrenia and other ciliopathies, is framed, not measured, here.

summaries.beginner: Tiny antennae on brain cells, called primary cilia, reach into the space around neurons and glia. A human cortex wiring volume shows they touch different partners by layer and cell type, and some even sit in the synapse itself.
summaries.intermediate: Wu et al. (Neuron, January 2024; DOI 2023) map the contactome and connectome of neuronal and astrocytic primary cilia in a 1 mm³ human temporal-cortex EM volume spanning all layers. Contacts, morphology, and microtubule axonemes vary by layer and cell class. Neuronal cilia can abut excitatory and inhibitory synapses; quantification versus axonal controls is significant (p < 0.05, t-test, as stated). The authors contrast this tetrapartite arrangement with the classical tripartite synapse. Catalog tags include MICrONS; the tissue is human cortex in the H01-class volume.
summaries.advanced: p < 0.05 is the only significance statement in the extract; effect sizes are in Figure 8. ‘Unique barcode’ is an interpretive summary of diversity, not a cryptographic identifier. Catalog dataset DS13 MICrONS is a graph-registry tag; this reconstruction is human temporal cortex with Lichtman/Jain authorship, not the mouse MICrONS cubic millimeter. Disease list in the discussion is associative.

plain_language_summary: Tiny antennae on brain cells, called primary cilia, reach into the space around neurons and glia. A human cortex wiring volume shows they touch different partners by layer and cell type, and some even sit in the synapse itself.

ocar.opportunity: Insect heading circuits are ring attractors with known connectivity; a vertebrate analog with both dynamics and EM architecture would close a mechanistic gap.
ocar.challenge: Vertebrate head-direction cells are well known physiologically, but the connectivity that implements a stable heading bump had not been reconstructed.
ocar.action: Petrucco, Lavian, Wu, Svara, Štih, and Portugues, in Nature Neuroscience (2023), use volumetric light-sheet imaging in larval zebrafish and EM reconstructions of the same stereotyped neurons.
ocar.resolution: A sinusoidal activity bump in the anterior hindbrain (rhombomere 1) rotates with directional swims and is stable for many seconds without landmarks, implying integration of turning efference. Somata sit dorsally; arbors enter the interpeduncular nucleus, where reciprocal inhibition is proposed to stabilize the ring attractor. The neurons are GABAergic and morphologically stereotyped, resembling fly central-complex heading networks.
ocar.future_work: The discussion notes nearby motor-related activity as a candidate integrator input. Full mapping of all attractor components comparable to the insect central complex is still lacking in vertebrates.

summaries.beginner: Larval zebrafish keep an internal compass of which way they are pointing. Imaging and electron microscopy find a small hindbrain circuit whose activity bump rotates with turns and is held in place by cells inhibiting each other.
summaries.intermediate: Petrucco, Lavian, Wu, Svara, Štih, and Portugues (Nature Neuroscience, 2023) describe a heading-direction network in larval zebrafish anterior hindbrain. Lightsheet volumes show a persistent rotating activity bump; EM shows stereotyped neurons arborizing in the interpeduncular nucleus with reciprocal inhibitory connectivity suited to a ring attractor. Persistence without landmarks is taken as evidence for efference-copy integration and an internal model of turning. Comparison to the fly central complex is explicit.
summaries.advanced: ‘Many seconds’ stability is the authors’ qualitative duration, not a single time constant in the extract. Reciprocal inhibition is from EM architecture plus dynamics, not a full connectome of every IPN neuron. Ring-attractor language is a model class, not a fitted parameter set here. Volume 26, May 2023, pp. 765–773.

plain_language_summary: Larval zebrafish keep an internal compass of which way they are pointing. Imaging and electron microscopy find a small hindbrain circuit whose activity bump rotates with turns and is held in place by cells inhibiting each other.

ocar.opportunity: Dopamine’s role in learning is conserved, but mammalian dopaminergic systems are too large to assign single identified neurons to a memory trace.
ocar.challenge: How dopamine encodes lasting yet flexible plasticity at cellular resolution remains hard to watch in real time in mammals.
ocar.action: McMillen and Chew, in Neuronal Signaling (2024; catalog year 2023), review dopaminergic contributions to learning, memory, and forgetting in C. elegans and survey dopamine-specific fluorescent biosensors plus optogenetic combinations.
ocar.resolution: The worm’s fully mapped connectome and small dopaminergic set (CEP, ADE, PDE) are presented as the place to dissect dopamine’s spatiotemporal logic. Biosensors (GRAB, FRET, cpFP-based) are proposed for whole-nervous-system imaging of memory traces. Insights are argued to be relevant to human learning-and-memory disorders because the signaling chemistry is conserved.
ocar.future_work: The sensors-plus-optogenetics program is prospective. Druggable-target language is a hope, not a screen result.

summaries.beginner: Dopamine helps animals learn, but in people it comes from huge groups of cells. This review says the worm’s tiny, fully mapped nervous system is a place to watch dopamine neuron by neuron as memories form and fade.
summaries.intermediate: McMillen and Chew (Neuronal Signaling, 2024) review dopamine in C. elegans learning, memory, and forgetting. They emphasize identified dopaminergic neurons and the complete synaptic connectome as experimental advantages over mammalian midbrain systems, and they outline fluorescent dopamine biosensors for real-time circuit imaging. Conservation of dopamine signaling is the bridge to human memory disorders. Open-access review; no new dataset.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review. CEP/ADE/PDE appear in the abbreviation list as the worm’s dopaminergic sensory neurons; do not treat that list as a new census. Biosensor use in learning assays is proposed. Catalog year 2023 versus 2024 journal volume reflects publication lag.

plain_language_summary: Dopamine helps animals learn, but in people it comes from huge groups of cells. This review says the worm’s tiny, fully mapped nervous system is a place to watch dopamine neuron by neuron as memories form and fade.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM and other biological 3D datasets outrun professional annotation; trained volunteers can segment organelles if tasks are well designed.
ocar.challenge: Zooniverse and similar platforms were not built as 3D microscopy workbenches, so teams keep rediscovering how to present stacks and QC volunteer labels.
ocar.action: Smith, King, Pennington, Tun, Basham, Jones, Collinson, Darrow, and Spiers, in Histochemistry and Cell Biology (2023), collate methods from Science Scribbler and Etch A Cell projects on Zooniverse into a primer covering project building, data collection, analysis, and management.
ocar.resolution: They report that image, video, and GIF presentations of volumetric data have yielded high-quality annotations in those collections (citing Spiers et al. 2021). Practical advice covers FOV tiling, ROI isolation, and not overwhelming volunteers with unbounded workloads. Limits include weak native 3D navigation compared with professional scrolling through planes.
ocar.future_work: Interactive multi-plane viewers, Bio-Formats support, and validation that added interface complexity does not drive contributors away are named development goals.

summaries.beginner: Huge 3D microscope volumes need more eyes than a lab has. This how-to explains how research teams have used the Zooniverse website so volunteers can help outline structures in those volumes.
summaries.intermediate: Smith et al. (Histochemistry and Cell Biology, 2023) write a methods primer on online citizen science for biological volumetric data, drawing on Zooniverse projects in the Science Scribbler and Etch A Cell families. They treat volunteer effort as a scalable annotation layer when analysis lags acquisition. Discussion emphasizes data presentation, tiling, contributor retention, and the platform’s limited 3D UI. Open access.
summaries.advanced: Annotation-quality claims cite prior project papers (e.g. Spiers et al. 2021), not a new accuracy table in this extract. This is not a connectome reconstruction. ‘Insurmountable volume of work’ is a recruitment risk, not a dataset size statistic.

plain_language_summary: Huge 3D microscope volumes need more eyes than a lab has. This how-to explains how research teams have used the Zooniverse website so volunteers can help outline structures in those volumes.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila’s mapped mushroom-body connectome and sleep genetics make it possible to ask which memory stages sleep helps, and through which cells.
ocar.challenge: Sleep–memory coupling varies with metabolic state, genotype, and memory type; deprivation methods can confound stress with sleeplessness.
ocar.action: Marquand, Roselli, Cervantes-Sandoval, and Boto, in Frontiers in Physiology (2023), review how sleep in flies supports acquisition, consolidation, and related processes, including switches between sleep-dependent and sleep-independent consolidation.
ocar.resolution: The review accepts that sleep facilitates learning in wild-type and memory-impaired flies, that deprivation impairs new acquisition, that sleep is central to consolidation, and that learning can itself increase sleep drive. Recent work is credited with neural substrates of sleep-dependent consolidation and with a switch that, in starved flies, favors sleep-independent consolidation. Individual sleep amounts vary widely (some flies as little as 4 min/day in a cited study).
ocar.future_work: Whether spontaneous short sleepers have memory defects, and cleaner deprivation devices, are highlighted. Alzheimer’s-model interactions are mentioned as a future setting.

summaries.beginner: Sleep helps fruit flies learn and lock in memories, but not always in the same way. This review gathers how fly sleep interacts with different memory stages and notes that hungry flies can switch to a sleep-independent route.
summaries.intermediate: Marquand, Roselli, Cervantes-Sandoval, and Boto (Frontiers in Physiology, 2023) review sleep’s benefits across Drosophila memory stages. They summarize that sleep prepares and consolidates memory, deprivation impairs acquisition, and learning can promote sleep. They highlight recent circuit-level accounts of sleep-dependent consolidation and of a starvation-gated switch to sleep-independent consolidation. Variability across individuals and assays is stressed. Review article.
summaries.advanced: The 4 min/day figure is from Geissmann et al. 2019 as cited, not a new measurement. ‘Evasive’ mechanisms in the abstract is the authors’ wording for still-incomplete molecular accounts. Catalog stages include acquisition/infrastructure; this paper is behavioral/circuit review, not an imaging-methods paper.

plain_language_summary: Sleep helps fruit flies learn and lock in memories, but not always in the same way. This review gathers how fly sleep interacts with different memory stages and notes that hungry flies can switch to a sleep-independent route.

ocar.opportunity: Tumor and epilepsy surgery routinely exposes cortical tissue that could feed human electrophysiology, organotypic culture, and volume EM if it is removed as a viable, oriented block.
ocar.challenge: Neurosurgical priorities (safety, oncologic margins) and the lack of a shared microdissection protocol have limited standardized human-tissue pipelines.
ocar.action: Straehle, Ravi, Heiland, Galanis, Lenz, Zhang, Neidert, El Rahal, Vasilikos, Kellmeyer, Scheiwe, Klingler, Fung, Vlachos, Beck, and Schnell, in Acta Neurochirurgica (2023), refine surgical principles over n = 36 experiments for removing cortical access tissue.
ocar.resolution: Seven principles: preparation under a minute, preserve cortical axis, minimize trauma, pointed scalpel, no cautery or blunt dissection, constant irrigation, retrieve without forceps or suction. After one teaching round, multiple surgeons obtained samples ≥5 mm spanning all layers plus white matter. 5–7 mm pieces suited acute slices and electrophysiology. No adverse events from sample resection were observed. Tissue went to carbogenated NMDG-aCSF or hibernation medium.
ocar.future_work: The note presents the method as enabling human-to-human translation, including volume EM that depends on preservation quality; it is not itself a connectomic reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: During brain surgery, a small piece of cortex is often in the way. This technical note tells surgeons how to lift that piece quickly and gently so scientists can still record from it or look at it with electron microscopy.
summaries.intermediate: Straehle et al. (Acta Neurochirurgica, 2023) describe microdissection of human cortical access tissue during tumor and epilepsy operations. Over 36 experimental rounds they standardized seven handling rules and showed that several surgeons could harvest ≥5 mm full-thickness samples, with 5–7 mm ideal for acute electrophysiology. Immediate immersion in cold carbogenated NMDG-aCSF or hibernation medium is specified. No resection-related adverse events are reported. Open-access technical note.
summaries.advanced: n = 36 is protocol-development rounds, not a clinical trial endpoint. ‘No adverse events’ is the authors’ safety statement for this series. Volume-EM use is cited from other human-cortex studies, not performed here. Ethical consent details are referenced but not reproduced in the extract.

plain_language_summary: During brain surgery, a small piece of cortex is often in the way. This technical note tells surgeons how to lift that piece quickly and gently so scientists can still record from it or look at it with electron microscopy.

ocar.opportunity: A gene-expression layer on a standard larval-zebrafish brain would let cell types, transgenes, traced neurons, and activity maps be queried in one space.
ocar.challenge: Prior atlases for this species lacked brain-wide, single-cell-resolution in situ RNA maps registered to anatomy and neuron tracings.
ocar.action: Shainer, Kuehn, Laurell, Al Kassar, Mokayes, Sherman, Larsch, Kunst, and Baier, on bioRxiv (11 Feb 2022), apply multiplexed HCR in situ hybridization for 200 marker genes, register them to the mapzebrain atlas, and add cfos activity maps from freely swimming larvae.
ocar.resolution: Expression, single-neuron tracings, transgenic lines, and anatomical segmentations can be co-visualized. As proof of concept they identify calb2a-expressing cerebellar eurydendroid cells that project to hypothalamus and are activated after food ingestion. The resource is meant to expand by community contribution.
ocar.future_work: Two hundred genes are an initial set, not a full transcriptome. Behavioral relevance of other labeled populations is left to users of the atlas.

summaries.beginner: Researchers painted 200 genes onto a standard map of the baby zebrafish brain. Overlaying those colors with cell tracings and a hunger-related activity gene revealed a new class of cerebellar cells that talk to the hypothalamus after a meal.
summaries.intermediate: Shainer et al. (bioRxiv, 11 February 2022) add multiplexed HCR RNA maps for 200 markers to the Max Planck Zebrafish Brain (mapzebrain) atlas, registered with neuron tracings, transgenes, and >100 anatomical segmentations. Immediate-early cfos maps from freely swimming larvae are included. The highlighted discovery is calb2a+ cerebellar eurydendroid cells projecting to hypothalamus and active after feeding. Preprint; CC-BY-NC 4.0.
summaries.advanced: 200 is the stated initial marker set. ‘Novel class’ is relative to prior larval zebrafish atlases as claimed by the authors. This is spatial transcriptomics registered to a light-microscopy atlas, not a synaptic EM connectome. Catalog stage tags (segmentation/proofreading) reflect atlas use, not an EM pipeline paper.

plain_language_summary: Researchers painted 200 genes onto a standard map of the baby zebrafish brain. Overlaying those colors with cell tracings and a hunger-related activity gene revealed a new class of cerebellar cells that talk to the hypothalamus after a meal.

ocar.opportunity: Raw cryo-EM movies and volume-EM/X-ray tomograms need a public home if reconstructions in EMDB/PDB are to be validated and algorithms trained.
ocar.challenge: Growth in 3D cell and tissue imaging plus cryo-EM has produced petabyte-scale raw data that journals do not host, and reuse is limited without rich metadata and segmentation archives.
ocar.action: Iudin, Korir, Somasundharam, Weyand, Cattavitello, Fonseca, Salih, Kleywegt, and Patwardhan, in Nucleic Acids Research (2023 database issue), describe EMPIAR (empiar.org): deposition, search, visualization, download, and a REST API.
ocar.resolution: At writing, EMPIAR held over a thousand entries totalling over 2 petabytes, covering raw cryo-EM and 3D reconstructions from volume EM and X-ray tomography. A 2021 vEM workshop recommended allowing segmentation-only entries linked to image data. FAIR analysis: DOIs of the form 10.6019/EMPIAR-XXXXX, open download, metadata still being enriched. PDBj mirrors the archive.
ocar.future_work: Data growth, curation load, optional linking to project-site stores for the largest sets, and richer metadata are the stated scaling problems. Deposition is generally not mandatory, unlike PDB/EMDB for many journals.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope movies and huge 3D cell images need a public library, not only the pretty reconstructed maps. EMPIAR is that library, already past a thousand datasets and two petabytes.
summaries.intermediate: Iudin et al. (Nucleic Acids Research, 2023; DOI 2022) present the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive. It stores raw cryo-EM frames and volume-EM/X-ray tomography reconstructions, with web and REST access. Scale at publication: >1,000 entries, >2 PB. Discussion covers segmentation archiving, regional mirroring (PDBj), and FAIR status. Catalog journal field lists bioRxiv; the PDF is the NAR database paper.
summaries.advanced: Entry and petabyte counts are a snapshot in the 2022/23 article and will have grown. ‘Over a thousand’ / ‘over 2 petabytes’ should not be treated as current API statistics. Segmentation-as-first-class-entries is a workshop recommendation described as not fully implemented in the extract. This is infrastructure, not a biological finding.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope movies and huge 3D cell images need a public library, not only the pretty reconstructed maps. EMPIAR is that library, already past a thousand datasets and two petabytes.

ocar.opportunity: If biological wiring topology carries computational bias, swapping a random reservoir for a connectome-derived matrix should change Echo State Network performance on a standard chaotic series.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear whether fruit-fly hemibrain topology helps, hurts, or merely stabilizes reservoir computers relative to a matched random sparse graph.
ocar.action: Morra and Daley (arXiv 2201.09359; IJCNN 2022 catalog DOI) replace the fixed random reservoir of an ESN with a connectivity matrix from a female Drosophila hemibrain (Janelia), train readouts with ridge regression on Mackey–Glass series, and compare to control ESNs (density 0.2) across four train-size and split variants.
ocar.resolution: In all four trial sets, the Fruit Fly ESN either significantly outperforms and has lower variance than the control ESN, or has lower variance alone. Training is readout-only; the reservoir is frozen.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s later pages are methods; specific MSE values should be taken from result tables. Whether synapse-weighted (not only topological) reservoirs matter is outside this extract.

summaries.beginner: A machine-learning reservoir is usually a random net. These authors drop in the fruit fly’s actual connection pattern instead and find it predicts a chaotic time series as well or more stably than the random version.
summaries.intermediate: Morra and Daley (arXiv, 23 Jan 2022; catalog venue IJCNN 2022) build Fruit Fly ESNs whose reservoir is a hemibrain-derived connectivity matrix (>25,000 neurons in the source reconstruction) versus a seeded random ESN with 20% density. The task is Mackey–Glass chaotic one-step (and farther-horizon) prediction. Across four data-size/split variants, FFESNs win on mean-squared error and/or variance. easyesn is used for implementation.
summaries.advanced: ‘Significantly outperforms’ is the paper’s summary; numeric MSE tables are not in the selected extract. Hemibrain completeness is ‘to date’ as of the 2022 text. Topology here is a (normalized) synapse-count matrix, not a biophysical neuron model. Variant A is a harder long-horizon split by the authors’ own account. Catalog DOI is IEEE IJCNN.

plain_language_summary: A machine-learning reservoir is usually a random net. These authors drop in the fruit fly’s actual connection pattern instead and find it predicts a chaotic time series as well or more stably than the random version.

ocar.opportunity: Heterogeneous synaptic weights in mouse V1 look messy across datasets; a compact circuit model fitted to visual responses could reveal ordered connectivity rules.
ocar.challenge: Cell-type- and layer-dependent connection statistics, plus experiment-to-experiment variability, make it hard to relate anatomy to visual computation.
ocar.action: Toyoizumi, in a PNAS commentary (2022), explains Kraynyukova et al.’s in vivo fit of a stabilized supralinear network (SSN) to mouse dLGN and V1 responses to gratings of varying contrast and orientation.
ocar.resolution: The SSN has thalamic weights gE, gI and recurrent JEE, JEI, JIE, JII plus a shared supralinear exponent n. Toyoizumi presents the companion paper as extracting V1 connectivity rules from population receptive-field averages despite heterogeneous connectome weights. The commentary is interpretive, not a new recording study.
ocar.future_work: Links to inhibitory stabilization, representational drift, and degeneracy in circuit parameters are cited as broader context. Catalog organism tags include C. elegans only as historical first-connectome background in the opening.

summaries.beginner: Mouse visual cortex wiring looks messy if you only list synapses. This short commentary explains a companion study that fits a simple excitatory–inhibitory network to real visual responses and reads ordered connection rules out of that fit.
summaries.intermediate: Toyoizumi (PNAS, 2022) comments on Kraynyukova et al. (PNAS e2207032119), who fit a stabilized supralinear network of V1 excitatory and inhibitory populations driven by dLGN to grating responses. Six weights plus a nonlinearity are the core parameters. The piece frames connectomics’ difficulty—high-dimensional, variable, hard to link to function—and treats the SSN fit as a way to find order in heterogeneous weights. Commentary, not original data.
summaries.advanced: Do not attribute Kraynyukova’s fitted weight values to this commentary; they are not in the selected extract. Catalog organism/dataset tags point at C. elegans; the scientific object is mouse V1. Figure-panel claims (e.g. gE < gI) appear as schematic fragments and should be verified in the companion paper.

plain_language_summary: Mouse visual cortex wiring looks messy if you only list synapses. This short commentary explains a companion study that fits a simple excitatory–inhibitory network to real visual responses and reads ordered connection rules out of that fit.

ocar.opportunity: A complete fruit-fly brain connectome lets one ask whether functional efficiency, robustness, and wiring economy emerge from a simple physical process on the anatomical graph.
ocar.challenge: Direct evidence that those three properties originate in connectivity has been limited by incomplete maps and missing theory.
ocar.action: Tian and Sun, in Network Neuroscience (2022), treat functional-connectivity formation on the fly brain as a percolation process controlled by the fraction of excitatory synapses λ (E/I balance).
ocar.resolution: Raising λ, a percolation transition appears at λ = 0.3 (E/I 3:7), where the advantageous properties emerge. Near λ = 0.5 (1:1) the giant strongly connected component’s size and growth reconcile, matching prior in vitro predictions of optimal E/I. Beyond λ = 0.6 (3:2) the properties saturate at bounds set by anatomical connectivity. Optimal λ ~ 0.5 is also tied to cortical criticality literature.
ocar.future_work: λ is defined as the excitatory synapse fraction with uniformly generated strengths; mapping onto measured fly E/I physiology is a modeling assumption. Human-brain rhetoric in the introduction is evolutionary framing, not a human connectome analysis.

summaries.beginner: Turn up the fraction of excitatory synapses on a fly brain map and, at a sharp point, the network suddenly becomes good at sending signals, surviving damage, and staying cheap to wire. That physics idea is called percolation.
summaries.intermediate: Tian and Sun (Network Neuroscience, 2022) analyze the then-largest fruit-fly brain connectome with percolation controlled by synaptic E/I balance λ. They report a nondilution percolation threshold at λ = 0.3 (3:7), an operating optimum near λ = 0.5 (1:1) aligning with Shew et al. 2011 in vitro work, and saturation after λ = 0.6 (3:2) set by static anatomy. Efficiency, robustness, and economy are treated as byproducts of the transition. Open CC BY 4.0.
summaries.advanced: This is a graph-physics study on an anatomical fly connectome, not a new EM reconstruction. λ values 0.3/0.5/0.6 are model parameters as defined (excitatory fraction), not patch-clamp ratios. ‘Largest yet’ is a 2022 claim. Catalog biological_application/fly tags match; ‘our brain’ in the introduction is rhetoric.

plain_language_summary: Turn up the fraction of excitatory synapses on a fly brain map and, at a sharp point, the network suddenly becomes good at sending signals, surviving damage, and staying cheap to wire. That physics idea is called percolation.

ocar.opportunity: Unlabeled EM slices are abundant; a two-stage semi-supervised scheme could make neuron segmentation work when dense labels are few.
ocar.challenge: Fully supervised deep nets collapse if the annotation budget cannot cover dense, complex neurites.
ocar.action: Huang, Chen, Xiong, Zhang, Chen, Sun, and Wu, in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (2022), pretrain by reconstructing volumes from perturbations, then regularize supervised training with pixel-level consistency between unlabeled images and perturbed copies (SSNS-Net).
ocar.resolution: On representative EM datasets they report up to 400% gain on the VOI metric versus supervised learning with few labels, matching a supervised model trained on ten times as much labeled data. Code is released.
ocar.future_work: Which datasets and label fractions produce the 400% figure must be read from tables not in the extract. Generalization beyond the tested EM volumes is not claimed in the selected text.

summaries.beginner: Drawing every neuron in an electron-microscope stack takes forever. This paper shows a network can learn from a handful of labels plus lots of unlabeled pictures, by insisting that slightly messed-up copies get the same answer.
summaries.intermediate: Huang et al. (IEEE TMI, 2022) propose two-stage semi-supervised neuron segmentation: perturbation-reconstruction pretraining, then consistency regularization on unlabeled EM. They state up to 400% VOI improvement over few-label supervised training, comparable to a model with 10× labeled data. GitHub: weih527/SSNS-Net. IEEE Xplore copy licensed to Johns Hopkins University in the extract footer.
summaries.advanced: 400% is the authors’ stated maximum VOI gain, not a mean across all splits. VOI is variation of information (lower is usually better in connectomics; treat the ‘gain’ as their reported relative improvement). Dataset identities are in omitted experiments. This is 2D/3D EM neuron segmentation, not proofreading software.

plain_language_summary: Drawing every neuron in an electron-microscope stack takes forever. This paper shows a network can learn from a handful of labels plus lots of unlabeled pictures, by insisting that slightly messed-up copies get the same answer.

ocar.opportunity: Linking human synapses (nanometres) through cells (micrometres) to the whole organ requires computing and storage that grow with every finer map.
ocar.challenge: The adult human brain has on the order of 86 billion neurons; a C. elegans-level structural–functional model does not yet exist for humans.
ocar.action: Amunts and Lippert, in Science (2021), as described in the catalog abstract, argue that big data from human brain structure push supercomputing, and that those demands may spawn methods useful beyond neuroscience.
ocar.resolution: The abstract contrasts the 302-neuron C. elegans connectome and proposed complete model with the still-distant human case, and treats decoding connectivity, signal transduction, and function as exponentially growing computational problems.
ocar.future_work: Creative computing solutions are invited; the abstract is a perspective, not a benchmark.

summaries.beginner: Mapping the human brain in fine detail creates more data than ordinary computers can handle. This short Science piece says that challenge may force new supercomputing ideas, using the tiny worm connectome as the completeness benchmark we do not yet have for humans.
summaries.intermediate: Amunts and Lippert (Science, 2021) discuss computing demands of human structural brain data. Per the catalog abstract, they cite ~86 billion adult human neurons versus the 302-neuron C. elegans connectome with a proposed structural–functional model, and they link multiscale connectivity research to exponentially growing storage and processing needs. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Verma et al., Journal of Comparative Neurology (2025), DHARANI: a 3D developing human-brain atlas of the second trimester, not the Amunts and Lippert Science perspective. The ~86 billion and 302-neuron figures above are from the catalog abstract (the 86 billion cites their reference 1). Independent reading of the 2021 Science piece is required.

plain_language_summary: Mapping the human brain in fine detail creates more data than ordinary computers can handle. This short Science piece says that challenge may force new supercomputing ideas, using the tiny worm connectome as the completeness benchmark we do not yet have for humans.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-mouse-brain images from STPT, fMOST, LSFM, VISoR, or MRI must sit in one atlas to type cells and assemble projection diagrams.
ocar.challenge: Cross-modal registration fails when anatomy, clearing, and modality-specific artifacts differ from the Allen Common Coordinate Framework (CCF).
ocar.action: Peng, Qu, Li, Xie, Liu, Wang, and many coauthors (Nature Methods, 2021; Research Square preprint in the extract) introduce mBrainAligner: coherent landmark mapping plus deep networks to align whole mouse brains to Allen CCFv3, and they build an fMOST-domain atlas.
ocar.resolution: They report whole-brain maps of 3D single-neuron morphology and cell types after registration. Comparisons versus MIRACL, ClearMap, and aMAP appear in figures for soma localization and axon mapping (e.g. 162 neurons with L1 apical dendrites; 63 VPM/VPL neurons in one panel). An fMOST average template is iterated and CCF annotations are back-projected.
ocar.future_work: Anatomical variation between fMOST and CCFv3 remains a registration residual. Precise numeric error tables should be read from the published Nature Methods figures.

summaries.beginner: Mouse brains imaged with different microscopes do not line up on the standard atlas by themselves. This method, mBrainAligner, uses landmarks and neural nets to warp whole brains into the Allen map so cells and axons can be compared.
summaries.intermediate: Peng et al. (Nature Methods, 2021; extract is a March 2021 Research Square preprint later published at the catalog DOI) present mBrainAligner for cross-modality registration of whole mouse brains to Allen CCFv3. Modalities named include STPT, fMOST, LSFM, VISoR, and MRI. They construct an fMOST atlas and map full single-neuron morphologies and cell types. Figure descriptions compare soma and axon accuracy with MIRACL, ClearMap, and aMAP.
summaries.advanced: The extract is a preprint; the version of record is Nature Methods 9 Dec 2021. Figure-caption neuron counts (162, 63) describe illustrated examples, not the entire BICCN corpus. ‘Coherent landmark mapping’ is the method name, not a claim of zero residual error. Catalog title says ‘cross-modal’; preprint title says ‘cross-modality’—same work.

plain_language_summary: Mouse brains imaged with different microscopes do not line up on the standard atlas by themselves. This method, mBrainAligner, uses landmarks and neural nets to warp whole brains into the Allen map so cells and axons can be compared.

ocar.opportunity: A subset of midbrain dopamine neurons also release glutamate; mapping that cotransmission from synapse to behavior could yield cell-type-specific therapies.
ocar.challenge: Functional roles of dopamine-neuron glutamate cotransmission were only emerging twenty years after its discovery, despite conservation across species.
ocar.action: Eskenazi, Malave, Mingote, Yetnikoff, Ztaou, Velicu, Rayport, and Chuhma, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2021), review synaptic, developmental, connectomic, and behavioral evidence for ventral-midbrain dopamine neurons that cotransmit glutamate.
ocar.resolution: Functional connectome mapping shows strong glutamate connections onto cholinergic interneurons in nucleus accumbens medial shell and lateral dorsal striatum. Glutamate markers in dopamine neurons peak embryonically and rise after toxins, suggesting a neuroprotective role. Behaviorally, cotransmission contributes to psychostimulant responses, positive valence, and cognition, with subtler negative-valence effects. Genetic pharmacotherapy (e.g. dopamine-neuron GLS1 reduction) is cited as a schizophrenia-relevant proof of principle.
ocar.future_work: Gene-therapy and intersectional targeting of cotransmitting subtypes are presented as future treatments for addiction, schizophrenia, and Parkinson disease, not as completed trials.

summaries.beginner: Some dopamine cells also spit out glutamate. This review traces that double signal from synapses to circuits to behavior and asks whether it could be a more precise drug target than dopamine alone.
summaries.intermediate: Eskenazi et al. (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2021) review glutamate cotransmission from ventral midbrain dopamine neurons. They synthesize in vitro discovery, in vivo confirmation across species, developmental regulation, and a functional connectome onto striatal cholinergic interneurons. Behavioral roles include psychostimulant responses and positive-valence/cognitive systems. Therapeutic framing covers addiction, schizophrenia, and PD, including Genetic Pharmacotherapy via GLS1. Review.
summaries.advanced: ‘Just over 20 years’ dates from the 2021 review. Connectome language here is functional/optogenetic mapping, not EM. GLS1 behavioral effects are cited from Mingote et al., not new data. Disease-treatment claims are translational outlook.

plain_language_summary: Some dopamine cells also spit out glutamate. This review traces that double signal from synapses to circuits to behavior and asks whether it could be a more precise drug target than dopamine alone.

ocar.opportunity: FIB-SEM sits in a resolution–volume niche that can quantify virus–cell architecture in 3D, not only 2D snapshots.
ocar.challenge: Virologists rarely have a practical map of room-temperature FIB-SEM: milling/imaging cycles, targeting, and how to turn volumes into viral-density statistics.
ocar.action: Baena, Conrad, Friday, Fitzgerald, Kim, Bernbaum, Berensmann, Harned, Nagashima, and Narayan, in Viruses (2021), write a primer on FIB-SEM in the vEM family and apply it to an in vitro SARS-CoV-2 infection study.
ocar.resolution: Automated mill-and-image cycles interrogate micron-thick samples at tens of nanometres or better. In the SARS-CoV-2 example, quantitation of viral densities and surface curvature shows virions preferentially at plasma-membrane regions of positive mean curvature. Data are in EMPIAR-10677; a supplementary movie reconstructs three infected Vero E6 cells.
ocar.future_work: The authors urge imaginative but realistic virology questions and warn that analysis, not acquisition, of giant volumes is the bottleneck.

summaries.beginner: A focused ion beam can peel a cell like a 3D onion inside an electron microscope. This primer shows virologists how that works and finds SARS-CoV-2 particles sitting on outward-bulging bits of the cell membrane.
summaries.intermediate: Baena et al. (Viruses, 2021) review FIB-SEM as volume EM for virus–cell architecture and include a room-temperature practical guide. Their SARS-CoV-2 in vitro analysis reports virions enriched at plasma membrane with positive mean curvature. Reconstructions of three Vero E6 cells and particle coordinates are deposited as EMPIAR-10677. Open-access review with a primary imaging component. Catalog tags include MICrONS/mouse; the study is cultured primate cells plus a methods primer.
summaries.advanced: ‘Tens of nanometers or less’ is the authors’ resolution band, not a measured voxel size in the extract. Curvature preference is for this in vitro Vero E6 infection, not tissue. EMPIAR-10677 should be used for quantitative reanalysis. Catalog organism/dataset tags are mismatched to the virology experiment.

plain_language_summary: A focused ion beam can peel a cell like a 3D onion inside an electron microscope. This primer shows virologists how that works and finds SARS-CoV-2 particles sitting on outward-bulging bits of the cell membrane.

ocar.opportunity: FIB-SEM can be wasted on the wrong cubic micrometres unless a fluorescently identified cell in a millimetre-scale specimen can be targeted at micrometre precision.
ocar.challenge: Automated vEM still struggles to find a specific labeled cell after heavy-metal embedding and trimming.
ocar.action: Ronchi, Mizzon, Machado, D’Imprima, Best, Cassella, Schnorrenberg, Montero, Jechlinger, Ephrussi, Leptin, Mahamid, and Schwab, in Journal of Cell Biology (2021), preserve fluorescence through preparation, trim using confocal maps of the resin block, and laser-brand landmarks to position FIB-SEM.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate targeted volumes of single identified cells in mouse mammary-gland organoids, Drosophila larval tracheal terminal cells, and adult Drosophila ovarian follicle cells, reporting ultrastructural details not previously appreciated. FIB-SEM is positioned for small isotropic volumes (3–4 nm voxels) versus SBEM for larger anisotropic volumes.
ocar.future_work: The paper is a tools workflow; throughput limits of serial mill-and-image remain. Catalog abstract is one sentence; biological findings are in the full figures.

summaries.beginner: Finding one glowing cell inside a big chunk of tissue, then milling only that cell in an electron microscope, is hard. This workflow keeps the glow, marks the block, and aims the ion beam with micrometre aim.
summaries.intermediate: Ronchi et al. (JCB, 2021) describe high-precision targeting for volume EM. Fluorescence is preserved in resin; confocal maps guide trimming; laser branding landmarks the FIB-SEM field. Applications: 3D cultures of mouse mammary organoids, Drosophila larval tracheal terminal cells, and adult ovarian follicle cells. They contrast FIB-SEM (fine isotropic milling, 3–4 nm class) with SBEM (larger volumes). Tools paper.
summaries.advanced: ‘Micrometer precision’ is the authors’ targeting claim. 3–4 nm is stated as achievable X,Y (and FIB Z) resolution in general, not a measured voxel size for every dataset here. No connectomic synapse graph is produced. Catalog abstract is extremely short; body text supplies the biological examples.

plain_language_summary: Finding one glowing cell inside a big chunk of tissue, then milling only that cell in an electron microscope, is hard. This workflow keeps the glow, marks the block, and aims the ion beam with micrometre aim.

ocar.opportunity: Primate prefrontal cortex is expanded; high-resolution anterograde and retrograde mapping in marmoset can show whether PFC is a mosaic of discrete columns plus broad diffuse axons.
ocar.challenge: Organization of local and long-distance PFC circuits, and how they differ from mouse, is only partly known.
ocar.action: Watakabe, Skibbe, Nakae, Abe, Ichinohe, Rachmadi, Wang, Takaji, Mizukami, Woodward, Gong, Hata, Van Essen, Okano, Ishii, and Yamamori, in Neuron (2023; catalog year 2021), perform high-resolution connectomic tracer mapping of marmoset PFC, including parcellation-free analyses and a mouse comparison.
ocar.resolution: Two projection styles: patchy submillimetre-scale columns in near and distant targets, and diffuse axons spreading widely in cortex and striatum. Patchy streams preserve PFC topography in parallel; diffuse projections overlap and vary in laminar spread. Reciprocal cortico-cortical patches are often precisely coextensive, supporting a mosaic of columns. Columnar projections are much less conspicuous in mice.
ocar.future_work: Whether each column is sharply bordered or blended, and how marmoset association areas correspond to macaque and human networks, remains partly open. Mesoscale variability may be stochastic or residual misregistration.

summaries.beginner: Marmoset prefrontal cortex sends two kinds of long-range wires: tight columns and a wide spray. The columnar style is much clearer in this primate than in the mouse, hinting at how primate frontal circuits are tiled.
summaries.intermediate: Watakabe et al. (Neuron, 2023; NIH author manuscript of a 2021 bioRxiv) map marmoset PFC corticocortical and corticostriatal projections. Patchy columns (submillimetre) versus diffuse widespread axons recapitulate PFC gradients locally and globally. Reciprocal anterograde/retrograde patches often coincide. A mouse comparison finds weaker columnar structure. The work is mesoscale tracer connectomics, not EM. PMC manuscript.
summaries.advanced: ‘Submillimeter’ is the stated column scale. Dual topography is an organizing interpretation supported by their figures, with acknowledged patch-distribution diversity. Closed-loop human homology is suggested via citations, not human tracer data. Catalog year 2021 vs Neuron 2023 is preprint-to-journal lag.

plain_language_summary: Marmoset prefrontal cortex sends two kinds of long-range wires: tight columns and a wide spray. The columnar style is much clearer in this primate than in the mouse, hinting at how primate frontal circuits are tiled.

ocar.opportunity: The cerebellum’s regular anatomy invites a reconstruct-and-simulate model that unifies scattered connectivity numbers and tests how mossy-fiber bursts travel from granule to Purkinje cells.
ocar.challenge: Structure–function–dynamics links remain elusive because experimental synapse counts are incomplete and interdependent.
ocar.action: De Schepper, Geminiani, Masoli, Rizza, Antonietti, Casellato, and D’Angelo, in Communications Biology (2022; catalog year 2021), build a morphologically realistic multi-compartment model of mouse cerebellar cortex (BSB framework) with placement and connection rules, then drive it with background and sensory-burst mossy-fiber input.
ocar.resolution: Simulations show mossy fibers entraining a column of activity from granular to molecular layer. After geometric/functional tuning, examples include ~25% of ascending axons contacting overlaying Purkinje distal dendrites (7,133 of 28,615 granule cells), 2.4 synapses per such contact, ~12% of each PC’s granule input from ascending axons (empirical 7–24%), and synapse ranks by dendritic size PC (~1,500) > Golgi (~900) > basket (~700) > stellate (~500). Gap junctions and Golgi–Golgi inhibition were increased to match firing ranges.
ocar.future_work: The model is a resource for local computation and behavioral correlates; pathological parameter sweeps are mentioned as compatible but not the extract’s focus. Full-length parallel-fiber scaling would increase synapse counts proportionally.

summaries.beginner: The cerebellum looks like a crystal, but the exact numbers of wires are still argued. A detailed computer reconstruction of mouse cerebellar cortex lets mossy-fiber bursts play through realistic cells and predicts how activity climbs toward Purkinje cells.
summaries.intermediate: De Schepper et al. (Communications Biology, 2022) reconstruct and simulate mouse cerebellar cortical microcircuitry with multi-compartment neurons and rule-based connectivity. Validation uses in vivo–like mossy-fiber background and bursts. They propose a model-based ground truth for several debated synapse numbers (ascending-axon versus parallel-fiber share onto Purkinje cells; molecular-layer interneuron pathways) and show columnar propagation from granule to molecular layer. Open access.
summaries.advanced: Synapse counts after ‘functional tuning’ are model outputs constrained by literature, not new EM censuses. 7,133/28,615 and ~12% are stated model figures; empirical 7–24% is cited. Golgi–Golgi 160 GABAergic synapses lacked an experimental counterpart. Catalog year 2021 vs 2022 publication. This is simulation, not a volume-EM connectome.

plain_language_summary: The cerebellum looks like a crystal, but the exact numbers of wires are still argued. A detailed computer reconstruction of mouse cerebellar cortex lets mossy-fiber bursts play through realistic cells and predicts how activity climbs toward Purkinje cells.

ocar.opportunity: When a serial-EM sample is rare or imaging conditions drift, the goal is to label the stack in hand, not to generalize to future volumes.
ocar.challenge: Standard supervised segmentation assumes enough labels and a generalization target; that is the wrong setting for small, unique series.
ocar.action: Takaya, Takeichi, Ozaki, and Kurihara, in Journal of Neuroscience Methods (2021), as described in the catalog abstract, propose sequential semi-supervised segmentation (4S): iterate train–infer–pseudo-label along the series, exploiting correlation between adjacent sections, from few teacher labels.
ocar.resolution: On two serial-section image types the abstract reports qualitative and quantitative gains versus supervised learning with few labels, and it examines how the number and position of teacher labels affect performance. The method is framed as a transductive extractor of neural regions from EM stacks.
ocar.future_work: The authors planned to embed 4S in a general-purpose annotation tool.

summaries.beginner: If you only labeled a few slices in a stack of electron-microscope pictures, you still want the rest filled in. This methods paper walks a network along the stack, using each slice to help the next, instead of pretending it must work on brand-new samples.
summaries.intermediate: Takaya, Takeichi, Ozaki, and Kurihara (Journal of Neuroscience Methods, 2021) introduce sequential semi-supervised segmentation (4S) for serial EM. Per the catalog abstract, the setting is transductive: predict all labels in a given stack from partial labels, using adjacent-slice correlation and iterative pseudo-labeling. Experiments on two serial-image types are said to beat few-label supervised learning, with an ablation on teacher-label number and placement. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Manor, Thiyagarajan, Harris, Sheridan and colleagues on sparse 2D annotations bootstrapping dense 3D neuron segmentation (Research Square-style extract), not Takaya et al. 4S. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Journal of Neuroscience Methods paper is required for datasets and metrics.

plain_language_summary: If you only labeled a few slices in a stack of electron-microscope pictures, you still want the rest filled in. This methods paper walks a network along the stack, using each slice to help the next, instead of pretending it must work on brand-new samples.

ocar.opportunity: The cortico–basal ganglia–thalamic loop is a fundamental motif; a mesoscale map of all nodes could replace a three-channel (motor, limbic, associative) cartoon with experimentally defined subnetworks.
ocar.challenge: That three-channel view cannot explain the basal ganglia’s many functions, and multi-synaptic outputs of fine striatal domains had not been fully followed through pallidum, nigra, thalamus, and back to cortex.
ocar.action: Foster, Barry, Korobkova, Garcia, Gao, and a large Mouse Connectome Project team, in Nature (2021), map outputs of 29 dorsal-striatal domains (defined by cortical input topography) through GPe, SNr, thalamus, and cortex.
ocar.resolution: They identify 14 SNr and 36 GPe domains and a direct cortico-SNr projection. The direct (striatonigral) pathway is more convergent than the more parallel indirect (striatopallidal) pathway, yet both from the same striatal domain meet on the same SNr neurons. Six domains in parafascicular and ventromedial thalamus define six parallel cortico–basal ganglia–thalamic subnetworks that return to the originating corticostriatal neurons in a closed loop.
ocar.future_work: Clinical implications for disorders of the loop are cited as motivation; this paper is anatomical mapping. Domain structure of pallidum/nigra is argued to match prior topography and physiology (including C. J. Wilson, personal communication) but is newly formalized here.

summaries.beginner: Textbook diagrams give the basal ganglia three channels. A mouse whole-system map finds six parallel loops, each returning to the same cortical starting point, with much finer neighborhoods in striatum, pallidum, nigra, and thalamus.
summaries.intermediate: Foster et al. (Nature, 2021) mesoscale-map the mouse cortico–basal ganglia–thalamic network. Starting from 29 cortical-input-defined striatal domains they report 36 GPe and 14 SNr domains, a cortico-SNr shortcut, greater convergence on the direct than the indirect pathway with recombination onto shared SNr cells, six thalamic domains, and six closed-loop subnetworks. Open-access Nature article. Tracer-based, not EM.
summaries.advanced: Domain counts (29/36/14/6/6) are the authors’ parcellations from this mapping series, including prior striatal work cited as reference 5. ‘Bona fide closed loop’ is their anatomical conclusion from thalamic return to originating corticostriatal neurons. Catalog method tag ‘Network motifs’ is conceptual; the data are anterograde/retrograde pathway tracing. Discussion cites disease literature without new patient data.

plain_language_summary: Textbook diagrams give the basal ganglia three channels. A mouse whole-system map finds six parallel loops, each returning to the same cortical starting point, with much finer neighborhoods in striatum, pallidum, nigra, and thalamus.
